Series::CalcAccessor::diff.malliavin¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::CalcAccessor::DiffAccessor::malliavin(
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& F, std::int64_t dim = 0) const

Series malliavin_path(
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& F, std::int64_t dim = 0) const

Series skorokhod(
    const std::function<Series(const Series&)>& u, double dt, std::int64_t dim = 0) const

What It Computes¶

Discretize a Wiener path into increments ΔW_1, …, ΔW_n. A functional F of the path is a function of those increments, and its Malliavin derivative is the gradient with respect to them:

D_i F = ∂F / ∂(ΔW_i)

malliavin takes the increments as the receiver and returns that gradient. It is computed by one reverse pass, however many increments there are. malliavin_path takes the path W (n + 1 samples starting at 0) as the receiver and differentiates with respect to its n increments, so F sees the path rebuilt from them.

skorokhod computes the Skorokhod integral (the divergence, adjoint of the Malliavin derivative) of a process u = u(ΔW) that may look into the future:

δ(u) = Σ u_i ΔW_i − Σ (∂u_i / ∂ΔW_i) Δt

For an adapted u the second sum vanishes and δ(u) is the Itô sum. For an anticipating u it is still defined. The two are linked by the duality E[F δ(u)] = E[Σ u_i D_i F Δt], the integration by parts that moves a derivative from a payoff onto a weight.

Parameters¶

  • The receiver holds the Brownian increments (for malliavin, skorokhod) or the path (for malliavin_path) along dim. Other axes are independent paths.

  • F returns one value per remaining index: it reduces the time axis.

  • u returns a process with the shape of its argument.

  • dt is the time step (for skorokhod).

  • dim is the time axis.

Examples¶

Example 1. F = W_T² depends on every increment equally; its derivative is 2 W_T on each one.

auto dw = pluss::make_series({0.3, -0.5, 0.2, 0.4});

auto d = dw.calc.diff.malliavin([](const pluss::Series& inc) { return inc.sum().pow(2.0); });

std::cout << "derivative " << d << "\n";
std::cout << "2 W_T = " << 2.0 * (0.3 - 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.4) << "\n";

Output¶

derivative pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8]
2 W_T = 0.8

Example 2. The maximum of the path. Only the increments up to the position of the maximum move it: here the maximum is the first sample after the start, so only the first increment has a nonzero derivative.

auto dw = pluss::make_series({0.3, -0.5, 0.2, -0.4});
auto path = pluss::Series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64).unite({dw.cumsum(0)}, 0);

auto d = path.calc.diff.malliavin_path([](const pluss::Series& w) { return w.amax(0); });

std::cout << "path       " << path << "\n";
std::cout << "derivative " << d << "\n";

Output¶

path       pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.3, -0.2, 0, -0.4]
derivative pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 0, 0]

Example 3. For an adapted integrand the Skorokhod integral is the Itô sum. Take u_i = W at the left end of step i.

auto dw = pluss::make_series({0.3, -0.5, 0.2, 0.4});
auto adapted = [](const pluss::Series& inc) { return inc.cumsum(0).sub(inc); };

auto delta = dw.calc.diff.skorokhod(adapted, 0.25);
auto ito_sum = adapted(dw).mul(dw).sum();

std::cout << "skorokhod " << delta << "\n";
std::cout << "ito sum   " << ito_sum << "\n";

Output¶

skorokhod pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-0.19
ito sum   pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-0.19

Example 4. An anticipating integrand. With u_i = W_T for every i, the Itô sum is not defined, but δ(u) = W_T² − T.

auto dw = pluss::make_series({0.3, -0.5, 0.2, 0.4});
const double T = 1.0;
auto anticipating = [](const pluss::Series& inc) { return inc.sum().expand({inc.size(0)}); };

auto delta = dw.calc.diff.skorokhod(anticipating, T / 4.0);

const double wT = 0.3 - 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.4;
std::cout << "skorokhod   " << delta << "\n";
std::cout << "W_T^2 - T = " << wT * wT - T << "\n";

Output¶

skorokhod   pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-0.84
W_T^2 - T = -0.84

Example 5. Many paths at once: time on axis 0, paths on axis 1. The derivative has the shape of the increments.

auto dw = pluss::series::randn({6, 3}, pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64), 7);

auto d = dw.calc.diff.malliavin([](const pluss::Series& inc) { return inc.sum(0).pow(2.0); });

std::cout << "shape of derivative [" << d.size(0) << ", " << d.size(1) << "]\n";
std::cout << "equals 2 W_T on each increment: "
          << d.sub(dw.sum(0).mul(2.0).unsqueeze(0).expand({6, 3})).abs().amax().item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

shape of derivative [6, 3]
equals 2 W_T on each increment: 0

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • skorokhod costs one reverse pass per increment. Use it for the grid sizes of a test or a sensitivity, not for millions of steps.

  • The Malliavin derivative here is the discrete derivative of the discretized functional. It converges to the continuous one as the grid is refined; on a coarse grid, compare against a known case before relying on it.

  • F must be differentiable in the increments. A functional with an indicator (a digital payoff) has derivative zero almost everywhere; that is the case for which the Malliavin weight is used instead of the pathwise derivative.

Summary¶

diff.malliavin differentiates a functional of a Brownian path with respect to its increments, and diff.skorokhod integrates processes that look ahead.
